_comment: Plain-language term definitions shown on hover in chat answers (BUILD_PLAN §5.2). Deterministic: the LLM never writes these. Each definition paraphrases the TY2025 chunk named in chunkId. A human must review every entry and set reviewed=true (BUILD_PLAN §12).

terms.definition: Your total income minus certain adjustments (like student loan interest); you subtract your deductions from it to get taxable income.
Your AGI with certain amounts added back; for most students it is just your AGI, and it decides whether income limits shrink a credit or deduction.
The part of your income that tax is figured on: your AGI minus your standard deduction (or itemized deductions) and certain other deductions.
All income you receive as money, property, or services that isn't exempt from tax.
Pay for work you actually do, like wages, salaries, tips, and taxable scholarship or fellowship grants.
Income you didn't work for, such as interest, dividends, and capital gains.
A set dollar amount that reduces your taxable income, so you don't have to list your actual deductible expenses.
Specific deductible expenses listed on Schedule A; you use them instead of the standard deduction only when they add up to more.
An amount that reduces the income you are taxed on, which lowers your tax indirectly.
An amount subtracted directly from your tax, reducing it dollar for dollar.
A credit that can lower your tax to zero, but any amount left over isn't paid back to you.
A credit that can give you a refund even if you owe no tax or had no tax withheld.
An education credit for qualified expenses of an eligible student in the first years of college; part of it can be refundable.
A nonrefundable education credit for tuition and related expenses for courses at an eligible school, with no limit on the number of years.
A refundable credit for certain people who work; it may give you a refund even if you owe no tax.
Income tax your employer takes out of each paycheck and sends to the IRS for you, based on your Form W-4.
The form you give your employer when you start a job so they know how much income tax to withhold.
A statement from your employer showing what you were paid and how much tax was withheld from your pay.
A form your school sends showing what you paid for qualified education expenses and any scholarships or grants.
Tax you pay yourself during the year on income that has no withholding, like self-employment income.
Social security and Medicare tax paid by people who work for themselves, like the amounts withheld from an employee's wages.
Running your own business or working as an independent contractor rather than as someone's employee.
The category you file under (such as single or head of household), based on whether you are married and your family situation on December 31.
A filing status for unmarried people who pay to keep up a home for certain other people, like a qualifying child.
A qualifying child or qualifying relative who someone else can claim on their tax return.
A child, such as a son, daughter, or grandchild, who lived with you more than half the year and meets certain other tests.
A relative or household member who isn't anyone's qualifying child and meets tests for income, support, and relationship or living with you.
A student enrolled for the number of hours or courses the school considers full-time.
A student pursuing a degree at a college or university, or attending certain accredited schools; only degree candidates can get tax-free scholarships.
Money given to help a student pay for school; it is tax-free only to the extent it pays for tuition, fees, and required course materials.
Money paid to help someone pursue study or research.
Tuition and certain related expenses required to enroll at or attend an eligible school; they never include room and board or travel.
A college, university, vocational school, or other school that can take part in federal student aid programs.
Housing and meal costs; scholarship money used for them is taxable.
Interest you paid during the year on a qualified student loan; you may be able to deduct some of it.
The yearly period you report income and expenses for; for most people it is the calendar year.
A non-U.S. citizen taxed like a U.S. citizen because they have a green card or meet the substantial presence test.
A non-U.S. citizen who doesn't pass the green card test or the substantial presence test, and so follows different tax rules.
A count of days you were in the U.S. that decides whether a non-citizen is treated as a resident for tax purposes.
A tax ID number the IRS gives to people who need one but can't get a social security number; you enter it wherever an SSN is asked for.
